newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SOCCER-GOLDEN BOY BROLIN GIVES UP, BACK TO LEEDS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GOLDEN BOY BROLIN GIVES UP, BACK TO LEEDS.

text.p: Swedish golden boy Tomas Brolin boards a plane to England on Monday to try to salvage a footballing career almost wrecked by his one-man battle with authority and his own inner demons.

Brolin, one of the top three European footballers in 1994, has seen his national and international career spiral into non-existence since he picked a battle with Leeds United and their then manager Howard Wilkinson.

The cherubic blond Swede had shown huge promise when he joined Leeds in November 1995 for 4.5 million pounds ($7.6 million) from Italy's Parma after playing a key role in Sweden's impressive 1994 World Cup performance, when they reached the semifinals.

But the gritty Yorkshire club and Wilkinson's uncompromising approach were a recipe for disaster for the tempestuous Brolin, who is accustomed to getting his own way with the Stockholm jet set, of which he is a glamorous member.

"For me Leeds is what it's all about and I'll be there in England when pre-season training starts on Monday," Brolin told reporters on Saturday at a soccer festival with his original amateur club the Finflo Flyers.
Wilkinson has long gone from Leeds, replaced by another dour manager, George Graham.
But Brolin, regularly photographed with supermodels or Sweden's future Queen, Victoria, appears to have decided the only way to get back into soccer is to adopt a more humble approach.
"I'm going as a craftsman. The only thing I'm thinking about is getting a place in the team," Brolin said.
After some glittering displays of individual ball skills in the American heat of the World Cup, Brolin's career has been on the skids since his clash with Wilkinson.
Wilkinson refused to release Brolin and Leeds even cut short a loan agreement with Swiss club Servette, insisting he would either be in Leeds and available or would not play at all.

Brolin resisted, saying he would rather give up the game than go back to Yorkshire. His form suffered, his natural tendency to put on weight resurfaced and he lost his place in the international side.
Earlier this year, Leeds and Parma agreed to let Brolin play in Italy for a loan period but Parma declined to sign him, saying Leeds' 3.0 million pounds ($5.1 million) price tag was too high.
"I feel good. The spring in Parma was a boost and I got the match practice I needed so badly," he said.
But Brolin has had little contact with Leeds and it is not known if he figures in Graham's plans for the coming premiership season.
Brolin popped into Elland Road last month for a medical but did not meet Graham. He also does not have anywhere to live in Leeds, although he is keeping his apartment in Parma.

The Swede last met Graham nine months ago when the two failed to agree on terms and Brolin said he would not return to the English club. "The atmosphere at the club has become a lot better," Brolin said.
Brolin still has 12 months of his three-year contract with Leeds to run. Graham appears set, one way or another, on getting value for money for the player. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
